agenda: Maintenance of international peace and security
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: As a premier global maritime nation and commander of EU Operation ASPIDES, Greece's primary objective is to safeguard commercial shipping, protect international seafarers, and uphold freedom of navigation under UNCLOS by sustaining the Security Council's active oversight and extending monthly reporting on Houthi attacks. The most contentious negotiations will centre on balancing Western language affirming the right to defend vessels with Russian, Chinese, and Algerian concerns over US and allied airstrikes in Yemen, as well as their persistent demands to link Red Sea de-escalation directly to developments in Gaza. By anchoring the draft firmly in the previously agreed text of Resolution 2739, Greece aims to preserve consensus and prevent a veto while keeping maritime security at the forefront of the Council's agenda.

messages.Algeria: Algeria remains committed to safeguarding maritime navigation and security in the Red Sea, but we cannot accept language that has been misused to justify military actions against the territory of Yemen, which risk derailing the Yemeni peace process. Moreover, the Council cannot continue to ignore the direct link between the escalation in the Red Sea and the ongoing tragedy in Gaza. We urge the penholders to address these persistent concerns to allow for Council unity.
messages.China: China has consistently called for an end to attacks on commercial vessels to safeguard maritime security in the Red Sea, which is vital for global supply chains. However, Council resolutions must not be misconstrued or abused by any State to justify unauthorized military strikes that violate Yemen's sovereignty and exacerbate regional instability. The draft must maintain strict neutrality, avoid validating specific unilateral or regional military missions, and address the genuine root causes of the crisis, foremost among them the ongoing conflict in Gaza.
messages.Denmark: Denmark strongly supports this timely draft resolution circulated by Greece and the United States. As a major maritime nation whose seafarers and merchant fleet depend on safe and open sea lanes, ensuring freedom of navigation under UNCLOS and halting unlawful Houthi attacks in the Red Sea are top priorities for us. We fully endorse the draft text as presented and encourage all Council members to support its swift adoption.
messages.France: France fully supports the draft resolution presented by Greece and the United States, which provides a timely and necessary extension of the reporting mechanism under resolution 2722. We particularly welcome the explicit recognition of the vital defensive contributions of European Union operation ASPIDES in protecting merchant shipping and upholding freedom of navigation in accordance with UNCLOS. France stands ready to vote in favour of this balanced text, which firmly condemns Houthi attacks while reaffirming the importance of regional de-escalation and the UN-led political process in Yemen.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the draft resolution and the extension of the reporting mandate, as maritime safety in the Red Sea and adherence to international law, including UNCLOS, remain critical priorities. However, effectively de-escalating the situation requires directly acknowledging and addressing the primary root cause fueling wider regional instability, specifically the ongoing conflict in Gaza. We urge the penholders to reflect this connection in operative paragraph 4 to ensure a balanced and comprehensive approach.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the preservation of maritime security and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea, which is critical to international trade. However, any lasting solution must address the primary driver of regional escalation, namely the devastating conflict in the Gaza Strip. We also urge caution that defense of maritime assets does not justify unilateral strikes that violate territorial sovereignty or precipitate wider regional conflict.
messages.Panama: As the world's largest ship registry and a maritime nation deeply committed to the freedom of navigation, Panama fully supports the draft resolution. Upholding international law, as reflected in UNCLOS, and safeguarding commercial shipping, global supply chains, and the lives of seafarers are vital national interests for Panama. We thank Greece and the United States for their leadership and stand ready to vote in favor of this text.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea fully supports the draft resolution circulated by Greece and the United States. As a major maritime trading nation, we attach the utmost importance to safeguarding navigational rights and freedoms and protecting international supply chains in accordance with UNCLOS. We welcome the extension of the Secretary-General's reporting mandate and stand ready to vote in favour of the text as drafted.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation cannot accept provisions that are routinely distorted by the United States and its allies to justify unlawful strikes against sovereign Yemeni territory. Any balanced text must address the actual root cause of maritime disruptions—namely, the catastrophe in the Gaza Strip—and avoid endorsing Western naval missions. Without these essential corrections, our delegation will not be able to support the draft.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone welcomes the draft resolution extending the vital reporting mandate under resolution 2722 (2024) and remains firmly committed to safeguarding maritime security, international commerce, and the safety of seafarers in the Red Sea. In line with our consistent position, we believe the Council must squarely address the root causes driving this crisis, specifically the ongoing war in Gaza, which fuels regional escalation. We also emphasize the necessity of preserving the Yemeni political process and ensuring unhindered humanitarian relief.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia warmly welcomes the draft circulated by Greece and the United States, particularly the recognition of EU Operation ASPIDES and the clear reaffirmation of navigational rights under UNCLOS, which are of paramount importance to maritime nations like Slovenia. We reiterate our unequivocal condemnation of the Houthis' ongoing attacks against commercial vessels and their disruption of critical supply chains. To align the text fully with established legal principles and prevent further escalation, we urge explicit reference to compliance with international humanitarian law and the preservation of humanitarian access for Yemen's civilian population.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft resolution and shares deep concern over the ongoing Houthi attacks, which disrupt vital commercial shipping and pose grave security and economic risks to the Horn of Africa and adjacent waters. As a coastal State along the Gulf of Aden, Somalia emphasizes that security efforts must explicitly encompass the Gulf of Aden and address the destabilizing flow of illicit weapons across the maritime corridor. We appreciate the penholders' focus on regional leadership and full respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all coastal States.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports this timely draft resolution circulated by Greece and the United States. It is imperative that the Council speaks with one voice to condemn ongoing Houthi attacks against international shipping, uphold navigational rights under international law, and renew the Secretary-General's vital reporting mandate. We stand ready to support its swift adoption without delay.
messages.United States of America: The United States is proud to co-sponsor this draft resolution alongside Greece. The continued, reckless Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels in the Red Sea threaten global supply chains, freedom of navigation, and the lives of innocent mariners. Extending the Secretary-General's reporting mandate is essential for the Council's continued oversight, and we urge all members to support this text swiftly.

steps.summary: As co-penholder, Greece revised the draft by incorporating constructive proposals from Slovenia, Somalia, and Sierra Leone regarding the Gulf of Aden, international humanitarian law, and humanitarian delivery safeguards, while clarifying the defensive nature of Operation ASPIDES and reinforcing respect for sovereignty under the UN Charter to address concerns raised by China, Russia, Algeria, and Pakistan. The resolution maintains established agreed language from resolutions 2722 and 2739 on root causes and the right to defend commercial vessels, securing broad support across maritime and regional partners while preventing any veto.

steps.summary: As penholder, Greece maintains Revision 1 without modifications. The draft enjoys solid cross-regional backing with 11 members confirmed in support, while preserving vital Greek national priorities regarding UNCLOS, the safety of commercial shipping, and EU Operation ASPIDES. China, Russia, Algeria, and Pakistan are expected to abstain, ensuring adoption without any veto.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria abstains in line with its established precedent on resolutions 2722 and 2739, as the draft resolution retains language on vessel defense that risks legitimizing military strikes against Yemeni territory and fails to explicitly address the conflict in Gaza as the primary root cause of regional escalation.
reasons.China: Consistent with China's past abstentions on resolutions 2722 and 2739, the draft still lacks necessary safeguards against the unauthorized use of military force and fails to explicitly address the underlying driver of regional escalation in Gaza. China maintains continuity in its voting position and reserves its explanation of vote for after the adoption.
reasons.Denmark: As a major seafaring nation with vital commercial shipping interests, Denmark steadfastly supports the protection of freedom of navigation, international maritime law under UNCLOS, and the renewal of reporting on Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.
reasons.France: France strongly supports the draft resolution as it reinforces international maritime security, upholds freedom of navigation under UNCLOS, expressly recognizes the vital defensive mission of EU Operation ASPIDES, and maintains Council pressure against ongoing Houthi attacks in the Red Sea.
reasons.Greece: As the co-penholder and a prominent maritime nation whose national interests and legal principles strongly align with upholding freedom of navigation under UNCLOS and supporting EU Operation ASPIDES, Greece votes in favour of its own draft resolution.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana consistently supports the maintenance of maritime security, the protection of commercial navigation under international law, and the extension of the UN reporting mechanism on Red Sea attacks, consistent with its votes on resolutions 2722 and 2739. As is standard practice, Guyana will deliver its explanation of vote after the adoption of the resolution rather than before the vote.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the resolution because safeguarding maritime security and commercial shipping is vital to international trade and national economic interests. While disappointed that references to the Gaza ceasefire and unilateral strikes were excluded, Pakistan votes in favour given the text's focus on extending reporting and upholding freedom of navigation, while placing its reservations on the record.
reasons.Panama: As the world's largest ship registry, Panama consistently champions freedom of navigation, the safety of seafarers, and the protection of international maritime trade under UNCLOS, making strong support for this resolution essential to our national interests.
reasons.Republic of Korea: As a major maritime trading nation, the Republic of Korea consistently supports the protection of freedom of navigation and the condemnation of unlawful Houthi attacks on commercial shipping, aligning with our previous votes on resolutions 2722 and 2739. Any explanation of vote will be delivered after the adoption in line with standard practice.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia abstained on resolutions 2722 and 2739 due to concerns over Western strikes on Yemen being justified under the guise of vessel defense and the failure to explicitly link Red Sea instability to the conflict in Gaza; as the penholders rejected Russia's amendments on these exact issues, Russia maintains its abstention.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone consistently supports resolutions defending maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea, having voted in favour of resolutions 2722 and 2739, and our concerns regarding humanitarian safeguards and addressing root causes are adequately reflected in the draft. In line with Council practice, Sierra Leone will deliver any explanation of vote after the adoption.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia consistently supports the protection of freedom of navigation, compliance with UNCLOS, and the cessation of Houthi attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea, while appreciating the inclusion of international humanitarian law references and Operation ASPIDES. In line with its previous votes on resolutions 2722 and 2739, Slovenia votes in favour and will deliver any remarks after the vote.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia strongly supports maritime security, the interdiction of illicit arms trafficking across the Gulf of Aden that affects regional stability, and the reaffirmation of coastal states' sovereignty. Having supported the draft during negotiations with its key priorities addressed, Somalia votes in favour.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports extending the reporting mechanism under resolution 2722, upholding freedom of navigation, and enforcing the arms embargo against the Houthis; per standard UK practice on this file, our delegation will deliver an explanation of vote after the adoption rather than before.
reasons.United States of America: As a co-sponsor of the draft resolution, the United States fully supports renewing the reporting mandate of resolution 2722 (2024), condemning ongoing Houthi attacks on commercial shipping, and reaffirming the right to defend maritime vessels in the Red Sea.

before.Algeria:
Mr. President,

Algeria will abstain in the voting on the draft resolution before us today. Our position remains consistent with our votes on resolutions 2722 (2024) and 2739 (2024).

Algeria reiterates its unwavering commitment to international law, the United Nations Charter, and the principle of freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which is vital for international commerce. However, we have consistently cautioned against language that can be misinterpreted or misused to justify unilateral military strikes that violate the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and risk dragging the entire region into a wider, uncontrolled conflict.

Furthermore, we deeply regret that this Council continues to ignore the undeniable root cause of the current escalation in the Red Sea: the ongoing devastating aggression in the Gaza Strip. Tensions in regional waterways cannot be decoupled from the atrocities unfolding in occupied Palestine. Lasting maritime security and regional stability cannot be achieved through military strikes or selective enforcement, but only through an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza and genuine support for a Yemeni-led, Yemeni-owned peace process under United Nations auspices.

Thank you.
before.Greece:
Mr. President,

As a leading maritime nation and a staunch advocate for international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), Greece is proud to have submitted this draft resolution alongside our co-sponsor, the United States. 

The persistent, unlawful attacks by the Houthis against merchant and commercial vessels transiting the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and adjacent waterways pose an unacceptable threat to the lives of innocent seafarers, directly undermine navigational rights and freedoms, and disrupt global supply chains and economic stability. Freedom of navigation is not merely a regional concern; it is a foundational pillar of global commerce and international peace and security.

This draft resolution builds squarely upon resolutions 2722 and 2739. It rightly demands an immediate cessation of all such attacks, reiterates the call for the immediate release of the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew, and reinforces the imperative to enforce the targeted arms embargo established under resolution 2216 to stem the flow of weapons to the Houthis. It also appropriately recognizes the purely defensive contributions of maritime security operations, including the European Union's Operation ASPIDES, which plays a vital role in safeguarding civilian vessels and protecting the maritime commons.

At the same time, the text emphasizes the necessity of restraint to prevent broader regional escalation, underscores the importance of addressing the root causes of regional tensions, and reaffirms our steadfast support for the United Nations-led peace process in Yemen and the unhindered flow of humanitarian aid.

Upholding maritime safety and international law is a collective responsibility of this Council. Greece will vote in favour of this draft resolution and urges all Council members to support its adoption. 

Thank you.
before.Pakistan:
Pakistan attaches great importance to the safety and security of international maritime navigation, the protection of innocent seafarers, and the unimpeded flow of global commerce through vital sea lanes, including the Red Sea. We condemn all attacks against commercial and merchant vessels and therefore support the technical extension of the reporting mandate before us today.

At the same time, my delegation regrets that our constructive proposals were not accommodated in the final text. Any enduring solution to the crisis in the Red Sea cannot be decoupled from its primary root cause: the ongoing catastrophe in the Gaza Strip. True de-escalation across the wider Middle East requires an immediate, unconditional, and permanent ceasefire in Gaza. Furthermore, we caution against unilateral military actions that risk further inflaming regional instability and undermining the United Nations-led peace efforts in Yemen.
before.Russian Federation:
The Russian Federation will abstain on the draft resolution before us. 

While we consistently support ensuring the safety and freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways in accordance with international law, we cannot endorse a text that perpetuates the flawed approach established in resolution 2722 (2024). Regrettably, the sponsors have chosen to ignore our constructive proposals and have once again preserved ambiguous language regarding the supposed "right of Member States to defend their vessels," which the United States and its allies continue to abuse as a pretext to justify their unlawful missile and bomb strikes on the territory of sovereign Yemen. Such aggressive unilateral military actions do not protect merchant shipping; on the contrary, they undermine Yemeni peace efforts and dangerously escalate regional confrontation.

Furthermore, the draft resolution fails to frankly address the true catalyst of the ongoing crisis in the Red Sea: the ongoing catastrophe in the Gaza Strip. Normalization of maritime security in the region cannot be achieved in isolation from an immediate and lasting ceasefire in Gaza. As our key concerns regarding international legal precision and root causes were disregarded, Russia cannot support this draft resolution.
before.Somalia:
Mr. President,

Somalia votes in favour of this draft resolution. As a coastal State bordering the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, Somalia is acutely aware of the vital importance of maritime security and the preservation of freedom of navigation in accordance with international law. 

The continued attacks against commercial vessels in the Red Sea and adjacent waters not only disrupt global supply chains and vital economic lifelines, but also jeopardize the security of our entire region. Furthermore, illicit maritime arms trafficking networks directly threaten peace and stability by funneling weapons across the Bab al-Mandeb and the Gulf of Aden, fueling conflict and extremist groups.

We welcome the draft resolution’s clear emphasis on respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of coastal States, enhancing regional cooperation to combat illicit arms flows, and addressing the root causes of regional tensions. We reaffirm the imperative of de-escalation, the protection of humanitarian assistance, and continued support for a comprehensive, Yemeni-led political process under United Nations auspices.

Thank you.
before.United States of America:
Thank you, Mr. President. 

The United States is proud to co-sponsor the draft resolution before us today, and we thank Greece for its leadership in steering these negotiations.

For over a year, the Houthis have continued their reckless, unlawful, and destabilizing attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and surrounding waterways. These attacks directly threaten the lives of innocent seafarers from across the globe, disrupt international commerce, drive up costs for essential commodities—including humanitarian aid—and flagrantly violate international law and the fundamental principle of freedom of navigation.

One year ago, this Council adopted resolution 2722 (2024), demanding that the Houthis immediately halt these attacks and release the *M/V Galaxy Leader* and its crew, who remain unlawfully detained. Six months later, we reaffirmed that mandate in resolution 2739 (2024). Regrettably, the Houthis have defied the Council's repeated demands, continuing to launch sophisticated missiles and unmanned systems against civilian shipping. 

The resolution we are voting on today extends the Secretary-General’s vital reporting mechanism through July 2025, ensuring the Council remains fully informed of developments on the water. It reaffirms the right of Member States, in accordance with international law, to defend their vessels against these attacks, and it calls for concrete cooperation to disrupt the illicit flow of weapons and materiel to the Houthis in violation of resolution 2216. 

No member of this Council should tolerate armed groups holding global supply chains hostage. The Security Council must speak clearly and with a unified voice. We urge all Council members to vote in favor of this draft resolution. 

Thank you, Mr. President.

after.China:
Mr. President,

The Chinese delegation abstained in the voting on the draft resolution just adopted. I would like to elaborate on China’s position.

First, the Red Sea is an important international shipping lane for goods and energy products. Maintaining peace and stability in the Red Sea and ensuring the safety of international navigation is essential to global trade and supply chains, and serves the common interests of the international community. China has consistently called on the Houthis to respect the right of commercial vessels of all countries to navigate the waters of the Red Sea in accordance with international law, to immediately cease all attacks on civilian vessels, and to release the crew of the *Galaxy Leader*.

Second, China has repeatedly emphasized that the Security Council has never authorized any State to use force against Yemen. No country should misinterpret or abuse international law and Security Council resolutions, nor use them as a pretext to launch military strikes against Yemen or infringe upon its sovereignty and territorial integrity. Regrettably, over the past year, certain countries have persisted in conducting unilateral military strikes against Yemen, which have not achieved their stated objectives, but have instead resulted in civilian casualties, destroyed infrastructure, and exacerbated security risks and volatility across the Red Sea. The text just adopted retains certain ambiguities that could be exploited to justify further military escalation, which runs counter to the goal of de-escalation.

Third, current tensions in the Red Sea are a prominent manifestation of the spillover effects of the conflict in Gaza. To resolve the Red Sea crisis, it is imperative to address its root causes. Pushing for an immediate, unconditional, and durable ceasefire in Gaza, ending the unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe, and implementing the two-State solution are the fundamental ways to prevent further regional escalation. 

China calls on all parties to exercise maximum caution and restraint, avoid actions that aggravate tensions, adhere to the general direction of political settlement, and actively support the Yemeni peace process under the auspices of the United Nations. China remains ready to work with the international community to continue playing a constructive role in promoting peace and stability in the Red Sea and the wider Middle East.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Denmark:
Thank you, Mr. President.

Denmark welcomes the adoption of today’s resolution, and we thank Greece and the United States for their leadership in bringing this important text forward.

As one of the world’s leading maritime nations, Denmark attaches the utmost importance to the preservation of freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of innocent seafarers across the globe. The rules-based international order, anchored in the United Nations Charter and international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), must be upheld without exception.

For more than a year, the Houthis have carried out persistent, unlawful, and reckless attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waters. These actions endanger human lives, undermine vital global supply chains, drive up shipping costs worldwide, and directly disrupt the delivery of essential commodities and humanitarian assistance. 

Denmark strongly condemns these continuous attacks and demands that the Houthis immediately cease all such hostile actions and release the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew. We reiterate the right of Member States to defend their vessels in accordance with international law.

We also welcome the resolution’s explicit recognition of the vital defensive contributions of maritime security operations, including the European Union’s Operation ASPIDES, to which Denmark remains firmly committed in safeguarding commercial vessels and restoring stability to this crucial maritime corridor.

Furthermore, we must address the means fueling these attacks. It is essential that all Member States strictly comply with the targeted arms embargo established under resolution 2216 (2015) and enhance practical cooperation to intercept the illicit flow of weapons and materiel to the Houthis.

Finally, while defending maritime security, we must avoid further regional escalation. Denmark remains fully supportive of the United Nations-led peace efforts headed by Special Envoy Hans Grundberg. A sustainable, inclusive political solution to the conflict in Yemen remains indispensable for long-term peace in the country and stability across the entire region.

I thank you.
after.France:
(spoke in French):

Mr. President,

France welcomes the adoption of this resolution and thanks Greece and the United States for their initiative and leadership throughout the negotiations.

For more than a year, the Houthis have carried out repeated and unacceptable attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. These attacks pose a direct threat to the lives of innocent seafarers, undermine navigational rights and freedoms guaranteed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, disrupt global supply chains, and inflict severe economic harm, particularly on developing nations and the countries of the region.

France reiterates its condemnation in the strongest terms of these destabilizing actions and demands that the Houthis immediately cease all attacks and unconditionally release the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew. 

In this context, France recalls the right of Member States, in accordance with international law, to defend their vessels against such attacks. We also welcome the resolution’s explicit recognition of the essential defensive contribution of the European Union’s maritime operation, EUNAVFOR ASPIDES. Alongside our European partners, France remains fully mobilized within this operation, whose strictly defensive mandate is to escort merchant vessels, protect freedom of navigation, and contribute to maritime safety in full conformity with international law.

To put an end to these attacks, the Security Council must address their material sources. All Member States must strictly adhere to the targeted arms embargo established under resolution 2216 (2015), and external support that enables the Houthis to acquire advanced weaponry and illicit materiel must immediately cease.

Finally, France urges all parties to exercise restraint to avoid any regional escalation. We reaffirm our full support for the mediation efforts of the United Nations Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, towards an inclusive, negotiated political settlement under United Nations auspices, while safeguarding the unhindered flow of humanitarian assistance to the Yemeni population.

Thank you.
after.Guyana:
Mr. President,

Guyana thanks the delegations of Greece and the United States for their efforts in leading the negotiations on this resolution. 

Guyana voted in favour of the resolution extending the reporting mandate established under resolution 2722 (2024). We continue to support the Council receiving objective, accurate, and timely reporting from the Secretariat on the situation in the Red Sea, as unlawful attacks against commercial and merchant vessels persist, posing serious risks to maritime safety, international trade, and the lives of innocent seafarers.

Guyana reiterates its firm commitment to international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which guarantees the navigational rights and freedoms of merchant vessels. The Security Council has a fundamental responsibility to uphold international peace and security and must respond firmly to threats to international shipping lanes. 

In this regard, we once again call upon the Houthis to immediately cease all attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and adjacent waters, and reiterate our demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the *MV Galaxy Leader* and its crew. 

At the same time, Guyana emphasizes that sustainable maritime security cannot be achieved in a vacuum. We underscore the urgent necessity of addressing the root causes fueling heightened tensions across the region, paramount among which is the ongoing conflict in the Gaza Strip. Guyana reiterates its consistent call for an immediate, unconditional, and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, full and unhindered humanitarian access, and strict adherence by all parties to international law, international humanitarian law, and relevant Security Council resolutions. 

Finally, we urge all parties to exercise maximum restraint to prevent further regional escalation and to safeguard the diplomatic efforts toward a lasting and comprehensive peace process in Yemen under United Nations auspices. 

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Republic of Korea:
Mr. President,

The Republic of Korea voted in favour of the resolution today, co-sponsored by Greece and the United States. 

As a major trading nation and one of the world’s leading maritime countries, the Republic of Korea attaches utmost importance to ensuring safe, free, and lawful navigation in accordance with international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and adjacent waterways are indispensable lifelines for global trade and energy transit. The continued, indiscriminate attacks by the Houthis against merchant and commercial vessels undermine the fundamental principles of freedom of navigation, jeopardize global supply chains, and place the lives of innocent seafarers in grave peril. Such unlawful actions cannot be justified under any circumstances.

We welcome that today's resolution strongly condemns these ongoing attacks, demands their immediate cessation, and reiterates the call for the immediate and unconditional release of the *M/V Galaxy Leader* and its crew, who have now been unlawfully detained for over a year.

Furthermore, we underscore the critical importance of strictly implementing the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015). Disrupting the illicit trafficking of weapons, materiel, and advanced components to the Houthis is vital to halting their capacity to threaten international shipping. 

At the same time, we urge all parties to exercise restraint to prevent further regional escalation. Sustainable security in the Red Sea is inextricably linked to broader regional stability, and we reaffirm our steadfast support for the United Nations-led peace process in Yemen and the unhindered delivery of vital humanitarian assistance to the Yemeni people.

The Republic of Korea hopes that the adoption of this resolution will reinforce the Council's resolve to safeguard international peace, security, and global maritime order.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Sierra Leone:
Mr. President,

Sierra Leone welcomes the adoption of the resolution extending the reporting mandate of the Secretary-General on the Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels in the Red Sea, in accordance with resolution 2722 (2024). We thank the co-penholders, Greece and the United States, for their leadership and constructive engagement throughout the negotiation process.

Sierra Leone voted in favour of the resolution in line with our consistent support for the principle of freedom of navigation, the protection of navigational rights of all Member States, and the safeguarding of the lives of innocent seafarers, in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and applicable international law. 

We remain gravely concerned by the ongoing attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways, which continue to disrupt international commerce, destabilize global supply chains, and impose substantial economic costs on developing economies. We reiterate our demand that the Houthis immediately cease all such attacks and release the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew.

At the same time, Sierra Leone strongly emphasizes that the Council must not lose sight of the root causes of these maritime tensions. A sustainable solution requires addressing the broader regional dynamics and conflicts fueling instability across the Middle East. Furthermore, we urge all parties to exercise maximum restraint and avoid actions that could lead to regional escalation or jeopardize the delicate Yemeni peace process under United Nations auspices. 

We underscore the vital importance of the Secretary-General’s continued monthly reporting to keep the Council credibly and objectively informed, and we reaffirm our commitment to constructive engagement on this critical file.

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Slovenia:
Mr. President,

Slovenia voted in favour of the resolution just adopted, and we thank Greece and the United States for their efforts in steering this process.

As a maritime country, with the Port of Koper serving as a vital hub for trade and the transit of goods to Central and Southeastern Europe, freedom of navigation and maritime security in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) are of paramount importance to Slovenia. 

We reiterate our unequivocal condemnation of the continued Houthi attacks against commercial and merchant vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waterways. These unlawful actions endanger the lives of innocent seafarers, disrupt critical global supply chains, and risk dragging Yemen and the wider region into further instability. We reiterate our call for the immediate cessation of these attacks and for the immediate and unconditional release of the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew.

Slovenia particularly welcomes the acknowledgment in the text of the vital defensive role played by international and regional maritime operations, including the European Union maritime operation ASPIDES, in safeguarding merchant vessels and preserving freedom of navigation in full compliance with international law.

At the same time, we reaffirm our consistent position that all actions must adhere strictly to international law, including the Charter of the United Nations, international humanitarian law, and international human rights law. Maximum restraint is essential to prevent a wider regional escalation. We must ensure that maritime tensions do not derail the delicate United Nations-led peace efforts in Yemen or impede the delivery of critical humanitarian aid to the Yemeni people. Finally, we underscore the urgent need to address the root causes of tensions across the region to achieve lasting peace and stability.

I thank you.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
Thank you, Mr. President.

The United Kingdom welcomes the adoption of this resolution and thanks Greece and the United States for their leadership in bringing it forward.

For more than a year, the Houthis have carried out persistent, reckless, and unlawful attacks against commercial shipping transiting the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden. These attacks threaten the lives of innocent seafarers, jeopardize vital global supply chains, drive up costs for food and basic commodities, and undermine the fundamental principle of freedom of navigation under international law.

Through today’s adoption, the Security Council has sent another clear and united message: these illegal attacks must stop immediately. We reiterate our demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the *Galaxy Leader* and its crew, who have now been unlawfully held for well over a year.

It is also vital that the international community addresses the illicit flow of advanced weapons and military materiel to the Houthis. All Member States must strictly adhere to their obligations under resolution 2216 (2015) and halt the proliferation of arms that fuels this destabilizing behaviour.

The extension of the reporting mandate will ensure that this Council remains fully informed of developments and threats to maritime security. The United Kingdom remains steadfastly committed to defending the freedom of navigation and protecting international sea lanes in accordance with international law.

Thank you, Mr. President.
